title: From pipeline to power: what will determine which data centre projects get built?
gist: Wood Mackenzie tracks 434 GW of planned US data centre capacity versus 78 GW under construction, arguing that headline pipelines overstate deliverable electricity demand. Project credibility (permitting, customers, capital, utility engagement) and power deliverability (e.g. PJM accredited risked supply ~80 GW below high-confidence large-load demand) will decide which projects get built, with 100+ sites already turning to around-the-meter generation.

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie is tracking 434 GW of planned data centre capacity in the US, while only 78 GW is currently under construction.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Connelly
insights.so_what: Only ~18% of the planned pipeline is under construction; discount headline data-centre load forecasts accordingly.
insights.quote: Wood Mackenzie is tracking 434 GW of planned data centre capacity in the US, while 78 GW is currently under construction.

insights.claim: Proposed US data centre capacity does not automatically translate into electricity demand; headline pipeline numbers only tell part of the story.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Connelly
insights.so_what: Investors extrapolating announced GW into utility load growth or power equipment demand risk overestimating it.
insights.quote: proposed capacity does not automatically translate into electricity demand

insights.claim: Data centre projects differ sharply in certainty: a newly announced development is fundamentally different from one progressing through permitting, securing customers and capital, or moving towards construction.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Connelly
insights.so_what: Stage-gate data-centre pipelines (announced, permitted, financed, contracted, under construction) to estimate realistic load.
insights.quote: A newly announced development is fundamentally different from one progressing through permitting, securing customers and capital, or moving towards construction.
insights.locator: Which projects are most likely to materialise?

insights.claim: Utility engagement, as projects move from initial requests towards firmer commitments for electricity supply, is an important signal of which data centre projects will materialise.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Connelly
insights.so_what: Track utility large-load agreements and firm supply commitments as leading indicators of real data-centre demand.
insights.locator: Utility engagement provides another important signal

insights.claim: Utilities facing growing queues of large-load requests must differentiate project certainty to determine when and where demand will emerge, while developers must prove credibility and a viable route to power.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Connelly
insights.so_what: Utility capex plans built on unfiltered large-load queues carry forecast risk; developers with proven power access gain advantage.
insights.locator: For utilities facing a growing queue

insights.claim: Data centres can move from concept to development faster than new generation and transmission can be built, and in constrained power markets that mismatch becomes a significant obstacle to project development.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Connelly
insights.so_what: Speed-to-power is the binding constraint; assets and sites with existing grid access or fast-build generation command a premium.
insights.quote: Data centres can move from concept towards development more quickly than new generation, transmission and other energy infrastructure can always be built.
insights.locator: Can projects secure enough power, quickly enough?

insights.claim: In PJM, Wood Mackenzie's view of accredited risked supply is around 80 GW below high-confidence large-load demand.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Connelly
insights.so_what: An ~80 GW gap in PJM points to sustained capacity-price pressure and opportunity for new generation and behind-the-meter supply in that market.
insights.quote: In PJM, for example, Wood Mackenzie’s view of accredited risked supply is around 80 GW below high-confidence large-load demand.

insights.claim: Commercially credible data centre demand is not necessarily deliverable demand, because grid supply may not be available on the required timeline.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Connelly
insights.so_what: Separate 'credible' from 'deliverable' demand in power-demand models; the difference determines both utility load and bypass-generation opportunity.
insights.quote: Commercially credible demand, in other words, is not necessarily deliverable demand.

insights.claim: Grid constraints do not necessarily kill data centre projects; instead they change how projects secure power, pushing developers to a broader range of supply arrangements.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Connelly
insights.so_what: Grid scarcity creates demand for onsite generation, storage and private supply deals rather than cancelling load.
insights.quote: Grid constraints do not necessarily mean projects disappear. Instead, they can change how projects secure their power.
insights.locator: What happens when the grid cannot meet the timeline?

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie is tracking more than 100 disclosed US data centre sites with around-the-meter generation configurations, including behind-the-meter onsite power and front-of-the-meter generation onsite or at nearby nodes.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Connelly
insights.so_what: 100+ sites confirm onsite/near-site generation is a real trend; beneficiaries include onsite generation equipment and developers.
insights.quote: Wood Mackenzie is tracking more than 100 disclosed US data centre sites with around-the-meter generation configurations
insights.locator: Large data centre developments are already exploring

insights.claim: Around-the-meter supply choices by large-load consumers add uncertainty to the timing, location and characteristics of future utility electricity demand.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Connelly
insights.so_what: Self-supplied data-centre load may bypass utility sales growth; temper utility load-growth assumptions where onsite generation is common.
insights.locator: These approaches add another layer to the demand picture

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie frames data centre demand in three tiers—potential demand, credible demand, and demand the energy system can realistically serve—and argues the next phase of growth will be shaped by which projects make it from pipeline to power, not by proposed capacity.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Connelly
insights.so_what: Use a potential/credible/deliverable funnel when evaluating data-centre-driven power and equipment theses.
insights.locator: Moving from potential demand to deliverable demand
